events.description: Ambassador Dobrynin returned to Moscow, possibly reinforcing the Soviet appraisal that SALT and arms control objectives were unattainable.
Soviet military intervention and invasion of Afghanistan.
Research for the report was completed.
US controls on energy equipment exports to the USSR.
Ambassador Dobrynin returned to Moscow
Execution of Prime Minister Amin during the Soviet takeover
Chinese Foreign Minister Huang Hua to visit Pakistan
Chinese invasion of Vietnam
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and execution of Prime Minister Amin; new regime installed in Kabul
Iraq strongly condemned the Soviet invasion publicly
Yugoslavia condemned the invasion; Minic described it as a blueprint for post-Tito Yugoslavia
Ceausescu criticized the USSR in New Year message to diplomatic corps
French CP leader Marchais dispatched to Moscow
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, whose implications for Soviet foreign policy are assessed.
Ceausescu's annual New Year's message to the diplomatic corps in Bucharest unmistakably criticized the USSR without naming it.
Secretary Brown's trip to China, which Soviet media were expected to present as the 'real threat' to Asian nations.
Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.
Sino-Soviet armed clashes along the Ussuri River.
Chinese invasion of Vietnam.
Secretary of Defense Brown's visit to Beijing.
Huang Hua's visit to Pakistan expected later in the month.
Admiral Gorshkov recently visited Hanoi.
Beijing abrogated the Sino-Soviet Friendship Treaty.
Sino-Soviet river navigation talks tentatively scheduled to begin.
Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin was executed during the Soviet takeover of Afghanistan.
Iraq publicly and strongly condemned the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan (described as last week).
South Yemen and Syria sent congratulations to the new regime in Kabul.
Conservative Arab states signed the initial request for an urgent UN Security Council meeting on the invasion.
Iran strongly condemned the Soviet intervention and resumed media criticism of the Soviets, while keeping the US as its main enemy.
The French Communist Party dispatched leader George Marchais to Moscow after the invasion.
CSCE session scheduled for Madrid later in 1980, where the Soviets intended to present European security proposals.
Sino-Soviet border clashes. Afterwards the Soviets maintained a dialogue with Beijing.
India expressed 'grave concern' over possible new US arms deliveries to Pakistan.
Soviet officials in Pakistan threatened that Islamabad's security position would be difficult if it did not stop aid to the Afghan rebels. Moscow urged Pakistan that it was 'not too late'.
Prime Minister Hafizullah Amin was executed during the Soviet takeover in Kabul.
South Yemen and Syria sent congratulations to the new regime in Kabul, the only radical Arab states to do so.
Iraq publicly condemned the Soviet invasion 'last week'. Conservative Arab states signed the request for an urgent UN Security Council meeting or voiced indignation.
The Moscow-based leadership of the Iraqi Communist Party decided to begin rebuilding its organization, followed by a revival of antigovernment activity in Iraq.
Egypt was reportedly preparing anti-Soviet measures, including reducing the Soviet diplomatic mission in Cairo.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, taken with expectation of wider geopolitical gains.
Ambassador Dobrynin returned to Moscow.
US imposed controls on energy equipment exports to the USSR.
Cuba withdrew from consideration for a UN Security Council seat after the Afghan invasion.
Ceausescu delivered his annual New Year's message to the diplomatic corps in Bucharest, unmistakably criticizing the USSR.
Secretary of Defense Harold Brown's trip to China, which Soviet media were expected to portray as the real threat to Asian nations.
Soviet Security Council vote on Iranian economic sanctions anticipated.
Soviet forces introduced into Afghanistan (invasion).
US controls on energy equipment exports to USSR.
Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia.
First Chinese invasion of Vietnam.
Admiral Gorshkov recently visited Hanoi.
Secretary of Defense Brown's visit to Beijing.
Chinese Foreign Minister Huang Hua's visit to Pakistan later in the month.
Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, which drew reactions from Iran, Western and Eastern Europe, and the Eurocommunist parties.
Iran strongly condemned the Soviet intervention and resumed media criticism of the Soviets, while saying the US remains its main enemy.
The French Communist Party dispatched its leader George Marchais to Moscow after echoing the Soviet line on Afghanistan.
Yugoslavs condemned the invasion openly; Milos Minic reportedly called it a blueprint for Yugoslavia after Tito's death.
CSCE session scheduled in Madrid later in 1980, where the USSR intended to set forth proposals on European security; the invasion could complicate them.
Secretary of Defense Harold Brown's upcoming trip to China, which Soviet media were expected to portray as the real threat to Asian nations.
Upcoming Soviet UN Security Council vote on Iranian economic sanctions, seen as a measure of how far Moscow will oppose US interests.

sources_cited: CIA National Foreign Assessment Center intelligence assessment, January 1980
key_claims: Soviet decisions on scope and timing of the intervention were dictated largely by the situation in Afghanistan.
Moscow likely calculated it had little to lose in relations with the US given the decline of detente.
Soviet leaders likely saw Czechoslovakia precedent as evidence that military force enhances worldwide influence.
A prolonged Soviet presence in Afghanistan would likely damage Moscow's standing in the Islamic world, especially among neighbors.
The longer the Soviets remain, the greater the temptation to pressure Iran and Pakistan.
Moscow's most worrisome consequence is closer Sino-American security cooperation.
CIA assesses Moscow concluded detente benefits were already lost, so the invasion cost little.
CIA expects China's response to be the most troublesome long-term.
CIA expects Moscow to pressure Pakistan to cut aid to the insurgents, possibly using Baluchi and Pushtunistan issues.
US and Chinese military aid would make Pakistan more likely to resist Soviet pressure and increase aid to insurgents.
Indian criticism is expected to be muted by dependence on Soviet aid.
CIA assesses a long-term Soviet presence in Afghanistan will raise Afghanistan-Pakistan tensions and tempt Moscow to exploit Baluchi and Pushtunistan issues.
Pakistan will be cautious about aiding Afghan insurgents and may flirt with improved relations with Moscow absent security guarantees.
Radical Arab states are unlikely to criticize the invasion publicly, while conservative Arab states and Iraq condemned it.
Iran's reaction was initially muted, but Soviet operations against Islamic guerrillas may prevent Soviet-Iranian reconciliation.
Reaction among West European Communist parties is mixed and unlikely to cause a split like Czechoslovakia in 1968.
Moscow may retaliate with measures against US interests and try to separate the US from its allies on reprisals and TNF.
A Yugoslav presidium member reportedly saw the Soviet action in Afghanistan as a 'blueprint' for what could happen in Yugoslavia after Tito's death.
Romania, and Ceausescu in particular, indirectly criticized the USSR, while Poland and Hungary were less supportive than East Germany and Czechoslovakia.
Moscow was expected to retaliate against US countermeasures with limited steps such as curbs on Jewish emigration, pressure on dissidents and reduced economic ties.
The Soviets would seek to use Arab opposition to Camp David and the intimidating effect of the invasion to undermine US positions in the Middle East and South Asia.
Moscow would try to separate the US from its allies, including over long-range TNF, and could escalate over the Caribbean, East Berlin and SALT if bilateral relations worsened.
